lead: A fibre-reinforced plastic (FRP) carries load along stiff, strong fibres held in a soft polymer matrix. One thin layer, a ply, is very stiff along its fibres and soft across them: it is orthotropic, and four elastic constants describe it. Wing skins, control surfaces and blades are stacks of such plies at chosen angles. This chapter estimates the ply constants from the fibre and matrix, builds the ply stiffness matrix along its fibres, and rotates it to the axes of the structure.
prereq: You need: Hooke's law with Poisson's ratio in plane stress, and the transformation of stress and strain to rotated axes.

sections.h3: Fibres, matrix and the orthotropic ply

blocks.text: An FRP is a matrix, usually epoxy, holding long thin fibres of carbon, glass or aramid. The fibres give stiffness and strength along their length; the matrix keeps them in line, passes load between them by shear and protects them. A ply is one layer, typically about 0.125 mm thick for carbon/epoxy. Axis 1 runs along the fibres, axis 2 across them in the plane, axis 3 through the thickness. A skin ply is in plane stress, σ<sub>3</sub> = 0, so only axes 1 and 2 matter.

With all fibres in one direction, the ply has three perpendicular planes of symmetry: it is orthotropic. In the plane four constants describe it: E<sub>1</sub> along the fibres, E<sub>2</sub> across, the major Poisson's ratio ν<sub>12</sub> (the contraction in 2 per unit strain in 1) and the in-plane shear modulus G<sub>12</sub>. Simple micromechanics estimates the first two from the fibre volume fraction V<sub>f</sub>:
E<sub>1</sub> = E<sub>f</sub> V<sub>f</sub> + E<sub>m</sub> V<sub>m</sub>,   1/E<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>f</sub>/E<sub>f</sub> + V<sub>m</sub>/E<sub>m</sub>
blocks.where: E<sub>f</sub> and E<sub>m</sub> are the fibre and matrix moduli (GPa); V<sub>f</sub> and V<sub>m</sub> = 1 − V<sub>f</sub> the volume fractions. Along the fibres both phases stretch equally (rule of mixtures); across them they carry the same stress in series (inverse rule).

blocks.text: The inverse rule is rough, and fails for carbon, whose fibres are soft across their length; measured values are used. A typical carbon/epoxy ply has E<sub>1</sub> = 140 GPa, E<sub>2</sub> = 10 GPa, ν<sub>12</sub> = 0.30 and G<sub>12</sub> = 5 GPa. G<sub>12</sub> and E<sub>2</sub> are low because the matrix carries them.

sections.h3: The four constants and the Q matrix

blocks.text: In its own axes the ply's stress–strain law has no coupling between normal and shear terms:

σ<sub>1</sub> = Q<sub>11</sub> ε<sub>1</sub> + Q<sub>12</sub> ε<sub>2</sub>,   σ<sub>2</sub> = Q<sub>12</sub> ε<sub>1</sub> + Q<sub>22</sub> ε<sub>2</sub>,   τ<sub>12</sub> = Q<sub>66</sub> γ<sub>12</sub>
blocks.where: σ<sub>1</sub>, σ<sub>2</sub> are the normal stresses along and across the fibres and τ<sub>12</sub> the in-plane shear stress (GPa or MPa); ε<sub>1</sub>, ε<sub>2</sub> the normal strains and γ<sub>12</sub> the engineering shear strain.

blocks.text: Q<sub>11</sub> = E<sub>1</sub>/(1 − ν<sub>12</sub>ν<sub>21</sub>),   Q<sub>22</sub> = E<sub>2</sub>/(1 − ν<sub>12</sub>ν<sub>21</sub>),   Q<sub>12</sub> = ν<sub>12</sub>E<sub>2</sub>/(1 − ν<sub>12</sub>ν<sub>21</sub>),   Q<sub>66</sub> = G<sub>12</sub>
blocks.where: The Q terms are the reduced stiffnesses, in the unit of E; ν<sub>21</sub> = ν<sub>12</sub>E<sub>2</sub>/E<sub>1</sub> is the minor Poisson's ratio.

blocks.text: The relation ν<sub>12</sub>/E<sub>1</sub> = ν<sub>21</sub>/E<sub>2</sub> keeps the matrix symmetric, so ν<sub>21</sub> is always the smaller ratio. Q<sub>11</sub> is not a modulus. E<sub>1</sub> and E<sub>2</sub> come from a uniaxial test in which the ply contracts freely sideways. Q<sub>11</sub>, Q<sub>12</sub> and Q<sub>22</sub> describe the state in which sideways contraction is fully prevented (ε<sub>2</sub> = 0), so the ply is stiffer, and Q<sub>11</sub> is slightly larger than E<sub>1</sub>. The word reduced refers to having set the through-thickness stress σ<sub>3</sub> to zero.

sections.h3: Rotating the ply to the structure axes

blocks.text: In a panel the plies lie at angles. Let x, y be the structure axes and θ the angle from x to the fibre direction, anticlockwise positive, with m = cos θ and n = sin θ. Transforming stress and strain gives the stiffness in x, y, written Q̄:

Q̄<sub>11</sub> = Q<sub>11</sub> m⁴ + 2(Q<sub>12</sub> + 2Q<sub>66</sub>) m²n² + Q<sub>22</sub> n⁴,   Q̄<sub>16</sub> = (Q<sub>11</sub> − Q<sub>12</sub> − 2Q<sub>66</sub>) m³n + (Q<sub>12</sub> − Q<sub>22</sub> + 2Q<sub>66</sub>) m n³
blocks.where: Q̄<sub>11</sub> is the stiffness along x; Q̄<sub>16</sub> couples direct stress along x to shear strain. Q̄<sub>22</sub> follows from Q̄<sub>11</sub> by swapping m and n, and Q̄<sub>26</sub> from Q̄<sub>16</sub> likewise.

blocks.text: Q̄<sub>12</sub> = (Q<sub>11</sub> + Q<sub>22</sub> − 4Q<sub>66</sub>) m²n² + Q<sub>12</sub>(m⁴ + n⁴),   Q̄<sub>66</sub> = (Q<sub>11</sub> + Q<sub>22</sub> − 2Q<sub>12</sub> − 2Q<sub>66</sub>) m²n² + Q<sub>66</sub>(m⁴ + n⁴)
blocks.where: Q̄<sub>12</sub> is the Poisson coupling term and Q̄<sub>66</sub> the shear stiffness in x, y.

blocks.text: Q̄<sub>16</sub> and Q̄<sub>26</sub> are zero at 0° and 90° and largest in between, near 30° and 60° respectively for this carbon/epoxy. They are extension–shear coupling: pull an off-axis ply along x and it shears as well as stretches. Q̄<sub>11</sub> falls very fast as the fibres turn away from the load. This is how a laminate is tailored: 0° plies for axial stiffness, ±45° plies for shear stiffness and to resist buckling, 90° plies for transverse loads.

figure.caption: The rotated stiffness of the worked example's carbon/epoxy ply. Q̄<sub>11</sub> falls from 140.9 GPa along the fibres to 44.3 GPa at 45° and 10.1 GPa at 90°; the shear stiffness Q̄<sub>66</sub> peaks at 36.2 GPa at 45°; the coupling term Q̄<sub>16</sub> is zero at 0° and 90° and largest near 30°.

spec.aria: Left: a square ply with fibre lines drawn at 30 degrees to the x axis, the fibre direction 1 marked and the angle theta between them. Right: a graph of stiffness in gigapascals against theta from 0 to 90 degrees. Q bar 1 1 falls from 140.9 at 0 degrees to 10.1 at 90 degrees. Q bar 6 6 rises from 5 to a peak of 36.2 at 45 degrees and falls back. Q bar 1 6 starts and ends at zero and peaks near 30 degrees at about 42. Points at 45 degrees read 44.3, 36.2 and 32.7.

examples.question: A glass/epoxy ply has fibres with E<sub>f</sub> = 72 GPa in a matrix with E<sub>m</sub> = 3.5 GPa, at a fibre volume fraction of 0.6. Estimate E<sub>1</sub> and E<sub>2</sub>.
steps: Check: E<sub>1</sub>/E<sub>2</sub> = 5.5. The matrix is a small part of the stiffness along the fibres, but controls it across them.

examples.question: A carbon/epoxy ply has E<sub>1</sub> = 140 GPa, E<sub>2</sub> = 10 GPa, ν<sub>12</sub> = 0.30 and G<sub>12</sub> = 5 GPa. Find ν<sub>21</sub> and the Q matrix. Then find Q̄<sub>11</sub>, Q̄<sub>12</sub>, Q̄<sub>66</sub>, Q̄<sub>16</sub> and the modulus E<sub>x</sub> for the ply turned to θ = 45°.
steps: At 45°: m = n = 0.7071, so m⁴ = n⁴ = m²n² = m³n = mn³ = 0.25.

Modulus along x of the free ply: 1/E<sub>x</sub> = m⁴/E<sub>1</sub> + (1/G<sub>12</sub> − 2ν<sub>12</sub>/E<sub>1</sub>)m²n² + n⁴/E<sub>2</sub> = 0.25 × (1/140 + 1/5 − 0.6/140 + 1/10) = 0.07571 GPa⁻¹, E<sub>x</sub> = 13.2 GPa.

traps: Taking Q<sub>11</sub> = E<sub>1</sub>. The difference is small here (0.6%), but for glass/epoxy with ν<sub>12</sub> = 0.3 and E<sub>2</sub>/E<sub>1</sub> = 0.2, ν<sub>12</sub>ν<sub>21</sub> = 0.018 and the error is nearly 2%; Q<sub>12</sub> is never ν<sub>12</sub>E<sub>2</sub> without the denominator.
Mixing up ν<sub>12</sub> and ν<sub>21</sub>. ν<sub>21</sub> = ν<sub>12</sub>E<sub>2</sub>/E<sub>1</sub> is the small one.
Writing Q<sub>12</sub> = ν<sub>12</sub>E<sub>1</sub>/(1 − ν<sub>12</sub>ν<sub>21</sub>). The numerator is ν<sub>12</sub>E<sub>2</sub>, about 3 GPa here, not 42 GPa.
Assuming Q̄<sub>16</sub> and Q̄<sub>26</sub> are always zero. They vanish only at 0° and 90°.

quiz.q: Define an orthotropic lamina and name its principal axes.
quiz.a: A thin layer with three perpendicular planes of material symmetry. Axis 1 is along the fibres, axis 2 across them in the plane and axis 3 through the thickness.

quiz.q: Why is E<sub>2</sub> of a unidirectional ply much lower than E<sub>1</sub>?
quiz.a: Along the fibres both phases strain together and the stiff fibres carry most of the load. Across them the load passes through fibre and matrix in series, so the soft matrix controls the stiffness.

quiz.q: A glass/epoxy ply has E<sub>1</sub> = 40 GPa, E<sub>2</sub> = 8 GPa, ν<sub>12</sub> = 0.26 and G<sub>12</sub> = 4 GPa. Find ν<sub>21</sub>, 1 − ν<sub>12</sub>ν<sub>21</sub> and Q<sub>11</sub>.
For the carbon/epoxy ply of the example, find Q̄<sub>11</sub> and Q̄<sub>16</sub> at θ = 30°.
A single ply loaded along x at 45° to its fibres shears as well as stretches. Explain, and say how a laminate avoids it.
quiz.a: At 45° Q̄<sub>16</sub> and Q̄<sub>26</sub> are large, so a direct stress along x produces shear strain: the soft matrix lets the ply distort towards the stiff fibre direction. Pairing each +45° ply with a −45° ply makes the coupling terms cancel, because Q̄<sub>16</sub> changes sign with θ.

beyond: Not for the exam. Better micromechanics (Halpin–Tsai) improves the estimates of E<sub>2</sub> and G<sub>12</sub>. Ply strength is checked with the Tsai–Wu criterion. Search for Halpin–Tsai equations.
